issues.issue: The aggregate limit is tied to "all Claims first made during the Policy Period", while Section II.C. deems Extended Reporting Period Claims made in the preceding Policy Period and Section V.A. deems interrelated Claims first made under a prior policy. The interaction of those deeming rules with this limit could require construction.

Claims arising from "Interrelated Wrongful Acts" are deemed one Claim first made on the earlier of first assertion or notice "under this Policy or any prior policy", a relation-back rule whose operation depends entirely on the elastic Section III.K. definition. Whether a later Claim is swept back out of the Policy Period is precisely what parties fight over.

The deeming rule can place a Claim actually made during the Policy Period outside coverage, which sits uneasily with Insuring Agreement I's promise to pay Loss from Claims "first made against the Insureds during the Policy Period". Reconciling the two requires reading one as subordinate to the other.

The single per-Claim Retention says nothing about how it applies when Section V.A. deems multiple Claims to be one Claim or when Loss is shared across Insureds. Whether one or several retentions apply is a familiar dispute this wording does not settle.

The Insurer has "both the right and the duty to defend" any Claim "alleging a Wrongful Act", but the same paragraph ends that duty after exhaustion or "the rejection of a settlement offer as described below", a condition whose trigger is stated only obliquely. When the defence obligation terminates is left to construction.

A duty to defend is difficult to square with Section V.C.'s bar on the Insureds incurring any Defense Costs without prior written consent and with Section V.B.'s requirement that the Insureds bear the Retention themselves. Who funds and controls the defence below the Retention is not resolved.

Consent "shall not be unreasonably withheld" supplies no standard for measuring reasonableness, and the Insureds are barred from incurring "any Defense Costs" without it. Both the consent standard and the sub-fifty-percent-of-Retention carve-out are open to argument.

The hammer clause turns on whether the Insureds "unreasonably refuse to consent" to a settlement the Insurer "recommends", neither of which is defined or made subject to any process. Whether a refusal was unreasonable is a construction and fact question built into the text.

The provision relates back "any Claim subsequently arising from such Potential Claim" without saying how closely the later Claim must correspond to the noticed circumstances. That link is the whole battleground in notice-of-circumstances disputes.

The relation-back operates against the Declarations legend and Insuring Agreement I, which condition coverage on the Claim itself being first made and reported during the Policy Period or Extended Reporting Period. Which provision controls a Claim first made after expiry is a genuine question.

Compliance with a detailed content list is made "a condition precedent to exercising their rights", but the provision does not say whether partial compliance forfeits the relation-back benefit of Section VI.A. The severity of the condition is left open.

Notice must be given "as soon as practicable, but in no event later than sixty (60) days after such Claim is first made", combining an elastic standard with a hard deadline without saying which governs. The same drafting tension appears in Insuring Agreement I.

Notices "must" be delivered by prepaid express courier, certified mail or fax, an exclusive list that excludes e-mail and ordinary mail, and the clause cross-refers to a non-existent "Item 711" instead of Item 11. Whether notice by another means is effective would have to be construed.

Notices are deemed received "upon actual receipt ... or one day following the date such notices are sent, whichever is earlier", so a notice is deemed received a day after despatch even if it never arrives, and actual receipt can almost never be the earlier date. The provision is self-defeating as drafted.

The condition compares "the total number of employees in such entity and any subsidiaries prior to such Transaction" against "ten percent (10%) of the total number of Employees", mixing undefined "employees" with the defined term Employees. The measurement date and which population is counted are both uncertain.

This automatic-Subsidiary test (10% of Employees) and the very next paragraph's temporary-cover test (post-Transaction headcount exceeding 110%) use different metrics, leaving transactions that fall between them unprovided for. The two subparagraphs are hard to harmonise.

The sentence reads "as for a period of ninety (90) days", a garbled construction, and grants insurance only when headcount "exceeds a hundred and ten percent (110%)", saying nothing about Transactions that fall short of that figure but exceed the 10% test in the preceding paragraph. The gap is visible on the face of the text.

The bar on cover for pre-acquisition Wrongful Acts is stated for entities insured "pursuant to paragraph (a) above", yet Insuring Agreement I covers Wrongful Acts "before or during the Policy Period" and Section III.U. already limits Subsidiary cover to acts after the entity became a Subsidiary. Which limitation governs an acquired entity is arguable.

The text reads "after such or acquisition", an evident omission, and the ninety-day grant is expressed only for acquisitions taking headcount above 110%, implying smaller asset acquisitions receive nothing even though their new hires would be Employees. Both the wording and the implied negative require construction.

On a change of control coverage "shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company", which directly contradicts Section VIII.C.1's unqualified right of the Parent Company to cancel during the Policy Period. The two provisions have to be ranked.

Cover for a former Subsidiary continues "until termination of the Policy", whereas Section III.U. defines Subsidiary as an entity qualifying "so long as" the ownership test is met and limits cover to acts after it became a Subsidiary. Reading the two together for a divested entity is not straightforward.

The statements are made "the basis of this Policy" and incorporated into it, warranty-style language whose consequence (avoidance, rescission or nothing) the provision never states. What follows from an inaccurate statement is left entirely open.

Incorporating the Application and prior-insurer application into the Policy is in tension with Section VIII.K.'s statement that "this Policy constitutes the entire agreement". Whether the Application forms part of the contract has to be resolved between them.

Knowledge is imputed to the Policyholder only from an enumerated group of officers including a "human resources manager or risk manager", titles that may not match actual roles and are not defined. Whose knowledge counts is an expressio unius question on the list.

Severability is granted only as between Insured Individuals, saying nothing about whether an Insured Individual's knowledge is imputed to the Policyholder, which Section VIII.B.1 addresses in the opposite direction. The two limbs of the same condition must be read together to work.

The Parent Company may cancel by "advance written notice ... stating when thereafter such cancellation will be effective", with no minimum notice period, unlike the Insurer's twenty-day requirement. How much notice is "advance" is undefined.
"The customary short rate basis" is not defined or calculable from the Policy, leaving the refund on a Parent Company cancellation indeterminate. That is a nameable vagueness in a payment obligation.

The excess condition is drafted only for "Loss arising from any Third Party Claim", so it says nothing about other insurance covering employment-practice Claims, and the escape from it depends on another policy naming this Policy Number. The limitation to Third Party Claims may be read as an implied negative.

"Intended to provide primary insurance" is a statement of intention rather than an operative obligation, so it is unclear whether it actually makes the Policy primary against other coverage. The single sentence has to carry work its wording does not do.

"Full compliance with all the terms of this Policy" as a condition precedent to any action is absolute on its face, with no materiality or prejudice qualifier. Whether an immaterial breach bars suit is a live construction question.

The Parent Company acts for all Insureds on notices "except the giving of notice to apply for any Extended Reporting Period", while Section II.C. gives the election right to the Policyholder or the Insured Individuals and requires notice "by the Insured". Who may validly elect the Extended Reporting Period is not settled between them.

The entire-agreement statement cannot easily be squared with Section VIII.B. and Section III.A., which incorporate the Application and prior-insurer applications into the Policy as part of it. Whether the Application forms part of the contract turns on which provision prevails.

The clause purports to prevent notice or knowledge from working a waiver or estoppel as to either party, yet Section VIII.B. makes the Insurer's reliance on the Insureds' statements the basis of the Policy and Section V.C. requires the Insurer's consent decisions. Its interaction with those reliance-based provisions is contestable.
